source_caption:
I don’t remember this scene from “Good Will Hunting” 🤔

Dogma is the kind of movie Hollywood probably wouldn’t make today.

Released in 1999, Kevin Smith’s dark comedy follows two fallen angels, Loki and Bartleby, who discover a loophole that could get them back into Heaven. The problem? If they succeed, their actions could undo God’s entire plan.

The cast is ridiculous in the best possible way: Ben Affleck and Matt Damon as the two angels, Alan Rickman as Metatron, George Carlin as a Catholic cardinal, Chris Rock as Rufus, and Linda Fiorentino as Bethany, a woman who gets pulled into the whole mess.

What makes Dogma so memorable is that it doesn’t really attack faith itself. It plays with religion, organized religion, free will, guilt and the idea of what it actually means to believe in something.

And somehow, beneath all the jokes, there’s a surprisingly sincere message about faith and humanity.

It’s funny, strange, irreverent, and completely unlike most studio comedies from its era.

source_details.synopsis: Dogma is a 1999 American fantasy comedy film written, co-edited, and directed by Kevin Smith. The film stars Ben Affleck, Matt Damon, Linda Fiorentino, Salma Hayek, Jason Lee, Jason Mewes, Alan Rickman, and Chris Rock. It is the fourth film in the View Askewniverse. The story revolves around two fallen angels who plan to employ an alleged loophole in Catholic dogma to return to Heaven after being cast out by God, but as existence is founded on the principle that God is infallible, their success would prove God wrong, thus undoing all creation. The last descendant of Jesus Christ and two prophets are sent by the angel Metatron to stop them. Dogma screened out of competition at the 1999 Cannes
